column7: Salvage Therapy for Prostate Cancer: AUA/ASTRO/SUO Guideline
column10: A man has biochemical recurrence after prostatectomy and salvage prostate bed radiation is being planned. His PSA is 0.28 ng/mL. What timing principle applies?
column13: Delay radiation until pelvic pain develops
column14: Use orchiectomy as the local salvage treatment
column15: Offer salvage radiation while PSA is still low
column17: Option E is correct. Salvage radiation after prostatectomy is more effective at lower PSA levels, and eligible patients should be offered salvage radiation when PSA is still low rather than waiting for a higher threshold. Option A is incorrect because waiting for PSA above 2.0 ng/mL risks missing the window where salvage radiation is most beneficial. Option B is incorrect because docetaxel does not replace prostate bed radiation for potentially local biochemical recurrence. Option C is incorrect because symptomatic progression is too late for optimal salvage timing. Option D is incorrect because orchiectomy is systemic androgen deprivation, not local prostate bed salvage. Teaching point: In post-prostatectomy biochemical recurrence, salvage radiation timing is an oncologic decision; lower PSA at treatment is associated with better outcomes. Source: American Urological Association. Salvage Therapy for Prostate Cancer: AUA/ASTRO/SUO Guideline.

column7: Clinically Localized Prostate Cancer: AUA/ASTRO Guideline
column10: A man with high-risk localized prostate cancer chooses definitive external beam radiation therapy. Which androgen deprivation plan should be offered?
column11: No ADT if conventional imaging is negative
column13: One month of ADT after radiation ends
column17: Option B is correct. High-risk localized prostate cancer treated with radiation should include long-course androgen deprivation therapy, typically 18 to 36 months. Option A is incorrect because negative metastatic imaging does not remove the radiosensitizing and disease-control role of ADT in high-risk localized disease. Option C is incorrect because one month is shorter than the recommended long-course approach. Option D is incorrect because ADT is part of definitive radiation planning rather than a rescue therapy in this setting. Option E is incorrect because docetaxel does not replace guideline-directed ADT with radiation. Teaching point: ADT duration is risk-stratified; unfavorable intermediate-risk disease uses short-course therapy, while high-risk localized disease warrants long-course ADT with radiation. Source: American Urological Association. Clinically Localized Prostate Cancer: AUA/ASTRO Guideline.

column7: Diagnosis and Treatment of Non-Muscle Invasive Bladder Cancer: AUA/SUO Guideline
column10: A fit patient with newly diagnosed high-risk NMIBC has a complete response after induction BCG. What maintenance plan is recommended if BCG is available?
column12: Single postoperative gemcitabine instead of maintenance
column13: Maintenance BCG for three years as tolerated
column17: Option C is correct. A high-risk NMIBC patient who completely responds to induction BCG should continue maintenance BCG for three years as tolerated when BCG is available. Option A is incorrect because induction alone undertreats high-risk disease after response. Option B is incorrect because a single perioperative chemotherapy dose is a different recurrence-reduction maneuver, not the high-risk maintenance strategy. Option D is incorrect because cytology is surveillance, not treatment. Option E is incorrect because complete response permits maintenance rather than automatic cystectomy in an otherwise suitable patient. Teaching point: BCG response status determines the next step; complete response supports maintenance, while persistent high-grade disease requires a different escalation pathway. Source: American Urological Association. Diagnosis and Treatment of Non-Muscle Invasive Bladder Cancer: AUA/SUO Guideline.

column7: Medical Management of Kidney Stones: AUA Guideline
column10: A recurrent calcium oxalate stone former has hyperuricosuria and normal urinary calcium despite diet changes. Which medication best matches this metabolic profile?
column17: Option E is correct. Recurrent calcium oxalate stone formers with hyperuricosuria and normal urinary calcium may be offered xanthine oxidase inhibitor therapy to reduce recurrence risk. Option A is incorrect because acetohydroxamic acid is reserved for infection stones when surgical options are exhausted. Option B is incorrect because suppressive antibiotics do not treat hyperuricosuric calcium oxalate physiology. Option C is incorrect because loop diuretics can increase urinary calcium and are not stone-prevention therapy here. Option D is incorrect because glucocorticoids do not correct hyperuricosuria-driven calcium oxalate recurrence. Teaching point: Calcium oxalate stone prevention is phenotype-specific; hyperuricosuria with normal urine calcium points to urate-lowering therapy, not thiazide or alkalinization by default. Source: American Urological Association. Medical Management of Kidney Stones: AUA Guideline.

column7: Medical Management of Kidney Stones: AUA Guideline
column10: A patient has recurrent struvite stones with persistent urease-producing infection. Surgical options for complete stone clearance are exhausted. Which adjunct may be offered?
column17: Option B is correct. Acetohydroxamic acid may be offered to patients with residual or recurrent struvite stones when surgical options have been exhausted. Option A is incorrect because allopurinol targets hyperuricosuria-related stone risk, not urease-producing infection stones. Option C is incorrect because potassium citrate alkalinizes urine and is not the adjunct for persistent struvite stone infection. Option D is incorrect because thiazides target calcium stone risk through urinary calcium reduction. Option E is incorrect because severe calcium restriction is not a struvite treatment and can be harmful for calcium oxalate risk. Teaching point: AHA is a niche infection-stone adjunct for exhausted surgical options, not a substitute for complete stone clearance when surgery remains feasible. Source: American Urological Association. Medical Management of Kidney Stones: AUA Guideline.

column7: The AUA/SUFU Guideline on the Diagnosis and Treatment of Idiopathic Overactive Bladder
column10: An older patient with OAB asks about antimuscarinic therapy because of concern for cognition. What counseling should guide medication selection?
column11: Discuss dementia and cognitive impairment risk
column12: Avoid beta-3 agonists because they cause dementia
column13: Use chronic antibiotics before any OAB drug
column14: Require cystoscopy before counseling about drug risk
column17: Option A is correct. Clinicians should discuss potential dementia and cognitive impairment risk when prescribing antimuscarinic medications for OAB, especially when the concern affects shared medication choice. Option B is incorrect because the cognitive-risk counseling issue is tied to antimuscarinic exposure, not beta-3 agonists as a class. Option C is incorrect because antibiotics do not treat idiopathic OAB. Option D is incorrect because routine cystoscopy is not needed before medication risk counseling in an uncomplicated OAB presentation. Option E is incorrect because augmentation is reserved for severely impacted refractory patients after less invasive treatments fail. Teaching point: OAB pharmacotherapy is not just efficacy matching; antimuscarinic cognitive risk can legitimately shift shared decision-making toward alternatives. Source: American Urological Association. The AUA/SUFU Guideline on the Diagnosis and Treatment of Idiopathic Overactive Bladder.

column7: The AUA/SUFU Guideline on the Diagnosis and Treatment of Idiopathic Overactive Bladder
column10: A man with BPH on an alpha blocker has persistent urgency incontinence consistent with OAB. PVR is acceptable. Which add-on option is guideline-concordant?
column17: Option D is correct. Men with BPH and bothersome OAB symptoms may be offered antimuscarinic therapy, beta-3 agonist therapy, or combination therapy with an alpha blocker when clinically appropriate. Option A is incorrect because chronic catheterization is not routine treatment for BPH-associated OAB symptoms. Option B is incorrect because radical prostatectomy is cancer surgery and does not treat urgency incontinence. Option C is incorrect because cytology is not OAB therapy. Option E is incorrect because augmentation is reserved for severely impacted refractory patients after less invasive options fail. Teaching point: In mixed BPH/OAB symptoms, storage symptoms may need OAB-directed pharmacotherapy rather than endless alpha-blocker escalation. Source: American Urological Association. The AUA/SUFU Guideline on the Diagnosis and Treatment of Idiopathic Overactive Bladder.

column10: An intermediate-risk microhematuria patient wants to avoid cystoscopy after counseling and accepts cancer-risk tradeoffs. What can be offered to help decide?
column11: Urine cytology or a validated urine-based tumor marker
column13: Empiric antibiotics despite a negative culture
column17: Option A is correct. In appropriately counseled intermediate-risk patients who want to avoid cystoscopy, urine cytology or validated urine-based tumor markers may be offered to help decide about cystoscopy, while ultrasound-based upper tract evaluation still proceeds. Option B is incorrect because cystectomy has no role in initial intermediate-risk evaluation. Option C is incorrect because antibiotics do not evaluate unexplained microhematuria when culture is negative. Option D is incorrect because renal and bladder ultrasound remains part of the intermediate-risk evaluation pathway. Option E is incorrect because dipstick alone is not adequate microhematuria follow-up. Teaching point: Urine markers are a shared-decision tool for selected intermediate-risk patients declining cystoscopy, not a blanket replacement for risk-based evaluation. Source: American Urological Association. Microhematuria: AUA/SUFU Guideline.

column7: Diagnosis and Management of Male Chronic Pelvic Pain: AUA Guideline
column10: A man with CP/CPPS has pain flares and negative cultures. He asks for repeated systemic steroid tapers. What should be avoided?
column12: Alpha blocker when voiding symptoms dominate
column17: Option C is correct. Long-term systemic glucocorticoids should not be used for male chronic pelvic pain syndromes because harms outweigh any unsupported chronic pain benefit. Option A is incorrect because multimodal pain management is appropriate when tailored to phenotype and patient goals. Option B is incorrect because alpha blockers can be appropriate when voiding symptoms are a major CP/CPPS feature. Option D is incorrect because pelvic floor assessment helps identify treatable myalgia or tenderness. Option E is incorrect because psychosocial assessment is part of comprehensive chronic pain care. Teaching point: CP/CPPS treatment should be phenotype-directed and multimodal, but chronic systemic steroid exposure is not a durable management strategy. Source: American Urological Association. Diagnosis and Management of Male Chronic Pelvic Pain: AUA Guideline.

column7: Recurrent Uncomplicated Urinary Tract Infections in Women: AUA/CUA/SUFU Guideline
column10: A reliable woman with recurrent uncomplicated UTI recognizes typical cystitis symptoms and can submit cultures promptly. What management option may be offered?
column15: Daily urine cytology for recurrence tracking
column17: Option A is correct. Selected recurrent UTI patients may be offered patient-initiated treatment for acute episodes while awaiting urine culture, provided the approach is individualized and cultures remain part of care. Option B is incorrect because indefinite fluoroquinolone suppression creates avoidable resistance and adverse-effect risk. Option C is incorrect because cystoscopy is not performed before each typical uncomplicated episode. Option D is incorrect because culture documentation remains important in recurrent UTI management. Option E is incorrect because cytology does not diagnose or track bacterial cystitis recurrence. Teaching point: Self-start therapy is a stewardship-compatible convenience strategy only when paired with reliable symptom recognition and culture-based follow-up. Source: American Urological Association. Recurrent Uncomplicated Urinary Tract Infections in Women: AUA/CUA/SUFU Guideline.
